tierWindow.goal: Understand what practice- and work-based learning is and recognise it as learning through doing real tasks in real or realistic settings.
tierWindow.cognitiveDemand: Recognition, recall, description and guided application (understand and identify).
tierWindow.taskComplexity: Well-defined, one idea at a time; settled distinctions such as learning by doing versus classroom study.
tierWindow.autonomy: High scaffolding; worked examples; feedback confirms and explains; frequent low-stakes checks.

decidedValue.priorExperienceAnchor: No prior experience of practice- or work-based learning is assumed. The learner is early in their studies and may have heard of placements or fieldwork without a clear sense of what counts as practice- and work-based learning or why it is valuable; teach from first principles.

decidedValue.signpostBody: The course has three short lessons. First, what learning by doing is: what practice- and work-based learning means. Second, the many forms it takes: how it looks across different subjects. Third, the benefits to you: why it is worth doing. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.
decidedValue.signpostInstruction: Work through the three lessons in order.
decidedValue.overview:
This short course is about practice- and work-based learning: learning by doing real tasks in real or realistic settings. By the end you will be able to explain what it is, recognise the many forms it takes across different subjects, and describe the benefits it offers you.

In many disciplines you will be expected to take part in practice or work-based learning at some point in your degree. Knowing what it is, and why it matters, helps you recognise it when it comes and make the most of the chance.
decidedValue.courseOutcomesFraming: Three course outcomes framed up front: explain what practice- and work-based learning is, recognise the forms it takes, describe its benefits.

practiceConnection.academic: Practice- and work-based learning is becoming a central part of higher education, as more courses build links with industry and professional practice. Whatever you study, there is a good chance you will meet it, as a placement, fieldwork, a live project or something similar. Understanding it now means you can recognise the opportunity and get more from it later.

grounding.note: W-OPEN states the three course outcomes and why they matter (AL-5)

decidedValue.whereNextBody: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the intermediate course looks at how to make the most of a placement or project, and the advanced course turns to reflecting on experience with Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle. Going wider: Reflective Practice, Understanding Learning, Assessment and Feedback, and Academic Writing all put this kind of learning to work.
decidedValue.summary: You have reached the end of the course. Practice- and work-based learning is no longer a vague phrase: it is learning by doing, and you know what it offers. You can explain what it is: taking part in real tasks, in a workplace or a work-like setting, rather than only studying them from the outside. You can recognise the many forms it takes, from placements and fieldwork to live projects and volunteering. And you can describe its benefits: authentic experience, practical skills, growing confidence, and a clearer sense of the professional you are becoming. Look back at the confidence check to see how far you have moved.

practiceConnection.academic: From here, practice- and work-based learning is something you can look out for across your degree. When a module offers a placement, fieldwork or a live project, you will know what it is and what it can give you. It is also what employers value: real experience, used skills, and someone who has already seen the workplace from the inside.

courseReferences.title: See pages 220 to 230 of Chapter 12, 'Learning by Doing: Practice- and Work-Based Learning', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).
